title: Capstone Part 1: Architect a Production GenAI System
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 1: Architect a Production GenAI System ##### The system that worked until it had users A team in Pune built an internal knowledge assistant over eight weeks. Agentic RAG, hybrid search, reranking, a nice Streamlit UI. In the demo it was excellent. They rolled it out to 400 employees on a Monday. By Wednesday it was unusable. Median latency had gone from 2 seconds to 31. The vector database was returning results from other departments because there was no tenant filter. Costs were running at ₹1.9 lakh a week against a budget of ₹40,000 a month. And when someone asked why an answer was wrong, there was no way to find out — no tracing, no request IDs, nothing. Every one of those failures was predictable from the architecture. None had been considered, because the design document was a Mermaid diagram of the happy path. **The difference between a demo and a production system is that a production system is designed against constraints** — QPS, latency SLA, cost budget, access control, and observability. Today is that design work. Part 2 ships it. ##### The design document This is your practical task, and it is the highest-leverage day of the capstone. Write it before any code. ```markdown # Enterprise Knowledge Platform — System Design ## 1. Problem and users Employees cannot find answers across 40,000 documents spread over Confluence, Google Drive, and a ticketing system. Search is keyword-only and department- scoped, so cross-functional questions take 20+ minutes of manual searching. Primary users: 400 employees across 6 departments. Secondary: support agents needing fast policy lookup during calls. ## 2. Scope IN: Q&A over indexed documents with citations; multi-hop questions; department-level access control; conversation memory within a session. OUT: Document editing; actions on external systems; real-time data; languages other than English and Hindi (v1). ## 3. Requirements ### Functional - Answer questions from indexed documents with clause-level citations - Refuse cleanly when the answer is not in the corpus - Respect document-level access control - Support follow-up questions within a session ### Non-functional | Requirement | Target | Rationale | |---|---|---| | Peak QPS | 8 | 400 users × 12 queries/day, 60% in a 3h window | | TTFT p95 | < 2.0s | Conversational threshold | | E2E p95 | < 8s | Users tolerate this for a researched answer | | Availability | 99.5% | Internal tool; 3.6h/month downtime acceptable | | Answer accuracy | ≥ 85% on golden set | Below this, users stop trusting it | | Hallucination rate | < 3% | Measured on unanswerable questions | | Cost | < ₹40,000/month | Approved budget | | Data residency | ap-south-1 | Internal policy; some HR documents | ## 4. Constraints - No customer PII, but HR documents contain employee personal data - Existing Postgres and Kubernetes; no new datastore without justification - One engineer, 6 weeks to production ``` **The non-functional table is what makes this a design document.** Every number in it constrains an architectural choice, and writing them down forces the constraints to be explicit rather than discovered in week nine. **Derive requirements from usage, not from ambition.** 400 users × 12 queries/day concentrated in three hours is 8 QPS peak — which is small, and knowing it is small changes every subsequent decision. ##### Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Web UI / Slack bot"] --> B["API Gateway
auth, rate limit"] B --> C["Cache layer
exact + prompt"] C -->|hit| Z["Return"] C -->|miss| D["Security context
from session"] D --> E["Query router
simple / complex / no-retrieval"] E -->|simple| F["Single-shot RAG"] E -->|complex| G["Agentic RAG loop"] E -->|no retrieval| H["Direct answer"] F --> I["Hybrid retrieve
tenant-filtered"] G --> I I --> J["Rerank top-25 → 5"] J --> K["Grounded generation
with citations"] K --> L["Output guard
PII, grounding"] L --> M["Response + trace_id"] subgraph INGEST["Ingestion — nightly"] N["Confluence / Drive / Tickets"] --> O["Extract + classify"] O --> P["Structure-aware chunk"] P --> Q["Contextual enrichment"] Q --> R["Embed"] R --> S[("pgvector
+ metadata")] end S --> I M --> T[("Langfuse traces")] M --> U[("Postgres: feedback")] ``` **Every component needs a one-sentence justification.** This is what stops architecture-by-accumulation: ```python ARCHITECTURE_DECISIONS = [ {"component": "pgvector, not a dedicated vector DB", "reason": "40k docs → ~180k chunks. Well within pgvector's range. " "We already run Postgres, so this is zero new infrastructure.", "revisit_if": "chunk count exceeds 2M or p95 retrieval latency > 150ms"}, {"component": "Hybrid search (pgvector + Postgres FTS)", "reason": "Corpus contains ticket IDs, policy numbers, and error codes " "that embeddings cannot match. Day 21's argument.", "revisit_if": "BM25 contributes < 10% of final results"}, {"component": "bge-reranker-base, self-hosted", "reason": "Largest single retrieval quality gain. 25 candidates adds " "~120ms, within the TTFT budget.", "revisit_if": "TTFT p95 approaches 2s"}, {"component": "Query router before the agent loop", "reason": "Day 25 measured agentic RAG at 3x latency. ~70% of queries " "are simple; routing keeps median latency low.", "revisit_if": "routing accuracy < 85%"}, {"component": "gpt-4o-mini primary, gpt-4o for complex", "reason": "Cost budget is ₹40k/month. Cascade with verification keeps " "80% of traffic on the cheap tier.", "revisit_if": "escalation rate exceeds 40%"}, {"component": "Langfuse self-hosted, not LangSmith", "reason": "HR documents mean traces may contain employee personal data. " "DPDP Act favours keeping it in-region and under our control.", "revisit_if": "operational burden exceeds one hour/week"}, ] ``` **The `revisit_if` field is the part people omit.** A decision without a trigger for reconsidering it becomes permanent by default, and half of them will be wrong within six months. ##### Capacity and cost model ```python from dataclasses import dataclass import math @dataclass class CapacityModel: n_users: int queries_per_user_per_day: float peak_concentration: float # fraction of daily volume in the peak hour peak_hours: float avg_prompt_tokens: int avg_output_tokens: int cache_hit_rate: float escalation_rate: float @property def daily_queries(self) -> int: return int(self.n_users * self.queries_per_user_per_day) @property def peak_qps(self) -> float: peak_queries = self.daily_queries * self.peak_concentration return peak_queries / (self.peak_hours * 3600) def monthly_cost(self, price_small_in=0.0125, price_small_out=0.050, price_large_in=0.21, price_large_out=0.84, rerank_inr_per_query=0.0008, embed_inr_per_query=0.0002) -> dict: billable = self.daily_queries * (1 - self.cache_hit_rate) small = billable * (1 - self.escalation_rate) large = billable * self.escalation_rate small_cost = small * (self.avg_prompt_tokens / 1000 * price_small_in + self.avg_output_tokens / 1000 * price_small_out) large_cost = large * (self.avg_prompt_tokens / 1000 * price_large_in + self.avg_output_tokens / 1000 * price_large_out) infra = billable * (rerank_inr_per_query + embed_inr_per_query) daily = small_cost + large_cost + infra return { "daily_queries": self.daily_queries, "billable_queries": int(billable), "peak_qps": round(self.peak_qps, 2), "daily_inr": round(daily, 2), "monthly_inr": round(daily * 30, 2), "monthly_llm_inr": round((small_cost + large_cost) * 30, 2), "monthly_infra_inr": round(infra * 30, 2), "inr_per_query": round(daily / max(self.daily_queries, 1), 4), } model = CapacityModel( n_users=400, queries_per_user_per_day=12, peak_concentration=0.60, peak_hours=3, avg_prompt_tokens=2400, avg_output_tokens=320, cache_hit_rate=0.28, escalation_rate=0.20, ) print(model.monthly_cost()) ``` **Run this before building.** If the projected cost is 4× your budget, you learn it on day one rather than in week seven, and the levers from Day 41 are design choices rather than emergency retrofits. **Sensitivity analysis is worth ten minutes:** ```python def sensitivity(base: CapacityModel, **overrides) -> dict: """Which assumption matters most?""" baseline = base.monthly_cost()["monthly_inr"] results = {} for field, values in overrides.items(): for v in values: variant = CapacityModel(**{**base.__dict__, field: v}) cost = variant.monthly_cost()["monthly_inr"] results[f"{field}={v}"] = { "monthly_inr": cost, "delta_pct": round(100 * (cost / baseline - 1), 1)} return results print(sensitivity(model, cache_hit_rate=[0.10, 0.28, 0.50], escalation_rate=[0.10, 0.20, 0.40], avg_prompt_tokens=[1200, 2400, 4000])) ``` Usually `avg_prompt_tokens` dominates — which tells you that reducing `top_k` (Day 41) is your highest-leverage cost decision, before you have written any code. ##### Repository structure ``` knowledge-platform/ ├── README.md # design doc, architecture, how to run ├── pyproject.toml # pinned dependencies ├── Makefile # make ingest / serve / eval / deploy ├── docker-compose.yml # local: app + postgres + langfuse ├── Dockerfile ├── .env.example │ ├── docs/ │ ├── design.md # the document from section 1 │ ├── architecture.md # diagram + decision table │ ├── runbooks/ │ │ ├── quality-regression.md │ │ ├── latency.md │ │ └── cost-spike.md │ └── data-handling.md # Day 42's compliance plan │ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py # FastAPI │ ├── config.py # pydantic-settings, one source of truth │ ├── security.py # SecurityContext, access control │ ├── router.py # query routing │ ├── retrieval.py # hybrid + rerank, tenant-filtered │ ├── generation.py # grounded generation, citations │ ├── guardrails.py # input/output guards │ ├── cache.py # tiered cache │ ├── versioning.py # SystemVersion, prompt versions │ └── observability.py # tracing, metrics │ ├── ingest/ │ ├── sources/ # confluence.py, drive.py, tickets.py │ ├── chunk.py # structure-aware │ ├── enrich.py # contextual retrieval │ └── build_index.py │ ├── eval/ │ ├── golden_set.jsonl # 120 cases, built BEFORE optimising │ ├── run.py │ ├── gate.py # regression gate │ └── baseline.json │ ├── tests/ │ ├── test_security.py # access control — the critical one │ ├── test_chunk.py │ ├── test_guardrails.py │ └── test_retrieval.py │ ├── k8s/ # manifests from Day 43 └── terraform/ ``` **`docs/` is not optional in a capstone.** The design document, architecture decisions, runbooks, and data-handling plan are what distinguish a production system from a working prototype — and they are what a reviewer reads first. **`test_security.py` is the test that matters most:** ```python import pytest from app.security import SecurityContext from app.retrieval import SecureRetriever @pytest.fixture def tenant_a_ctx(): return SecurityContext(user_id="u1", tenant_id="engineering", roles=frozenset({"employee"}), document_groups=frozenset({"eng-public", "eng-internal"})) def test_cannot_retrieve_other_department_documents(retriever, tenant_a_ctx): """The Pune failure, as a test.""" chunks = retriever.retrieve( "summarise all salary bands across departments", tenant_a_ctx, k=20) for c in chunks: assert c["metadata"]["tenant_id"] == "engineering" def test_cannot_retrieve_restricted_group(retriever, tenant_a_ctx): chunks = retriever.retrieve("performance review policy", tenant_a_ctx, k=20) for c in chunks: assert c["metadata"]["access_group"] in tenant_a_ctx.document_groups def test_post_verification_catches_filter_bug(retriever_with_broken_filter, tenant_a_ctx, audit_log): """If the pre-filter fails, post-verification must catch it.""" chunks = retriever_with_broken_filter.retrieve("anything", tenant_a_ctx, k=10) assert all(c["metadata"]["tenant_id"] == "engineering" for c in chunks) assert any(e["event"] == "access_control_bypass_caught" for e in audit_log.records) ``` **That third test is the one worth writing.** It verifies your defence-in-depth actually defends, by deliberately breaking the primary control. ##### Configuration and versioning ```python # app/config.py from functools import lru_cache from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings from pydantic import Field class Settings(BaseSettings): # Secrets — no defaults, fail fast if missing database_url: str openai_api_key: str langfuse_secret_key: str langfuse_public_key: str # Models — pinned snapshots, never aliases (Day 35) llm_small: str = "gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18" llm_large: str = "gpt-4o-2024-11-20" embedding_model: str = "BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5" embedding_revision: str = "a5beb1e3e68b9ab74eb54cfd186867f64f240e1a" reranker_model: str = "BAAI/bge-reranker-base" # Retrieval — every number here is an experiment result, not a guess chunk_size: int = 800 chunk_overlap: int = 150 retrieval_candidates: int = 25 retrieval_top_k: int = 5 hybrid_bm25_weight: float = 1.0 hybrid_dense_weight: float = 1.0 # Generation temperature: float = 0.0 max_tokens: int = 500 # Budgets max_agent_iterations: int = 4 daily_cost_cap_inr: float = 1500.0 request_timeout_s: float = 30.0 # Cache prompt_version: str = "v3" exact_cache_ttl_s: int = 86400 semantic_cache_threshold: float = 0.97 class Config: env_file = ".env" @lru_cache def get_settings() -> Settings: return Settings() ``` **Fail fast on missing secrets.** A container that boots and then 500s on the first request is worse than one that refuses to start with a clear error. **Every retrieval number should be traceable to an experiment.** `retrieval_top_k: 5` because the Day 41 sweep showed quality peaks there — not because 5 seemed reasonable. ##### The core pipeline ```python # app/pipeline.py import time import uuid from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Optional @dataclass class QueryResult: answer: str citations: list[dict] trace_id: str request_id: str route: str cache_status: str cost_inr: float latency_ms: float system_fingerprint: str class KnowledgePlatform: def __init__(self, retriever, reranker, generator, router, cache, guards, version, tracer, budget): self.retriever, self.reranker = retriever, reranker self.generator, self.router = generator, router self.cache, self.guards = cache, guards self.version, self.tracer, self.budget = version, tracer, budget async def answer(self, question: str, ctx, session_id: str) -> QueryResult: request_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) t0 = time.perf_counter() trace = self.tracer.trace( name="knowledge_query", user_id=ctx.user_id, session_id=session_id, input={"question": question}, metadata={**self.version.as_tags(), "tenant": ctx.tenant_id, "request_id": request_id}) self.budget.check(ctx.tenant_id) guard = self.guards.check_input(question) if not guard.allowed: trace.update(output={"blocked": guard.stage}) return self._blocked(request_id, trace.id, guard, t0) cached = await self.cache.get(question, ctx, self.version.fingerprint) if cached: return QueryResult( answer=cached["answer"], citations=cached["citations"], trace_id=trace.id, request_id=request_id, route="cache", cache_status=cached["hit"], cost_inr=0.0, latency_ms=round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1), system_fingerprint=self.version.fingerprint) route = await self.router.route(question, session_id) trace.span(name="route").end(output={"route": route}) if route == "no_retrieval": result = await self.generator.direct(question, session_id) elif route == "simple": result = await self._single_shot(question, ctx, trace) else: result = await self._agentic(question, ctx, trace) out_guard = self.guards.check_output( result["answer"], context=result.get("context", "")) if not out_guard.allowed: trace.update(output={"blocked": out_guard.stage}) return self._blocked(request_id, trace.id, out_guard, t0) await self.cache.put(question, ctx, result, self.version.fingerprint) self.budget.record(ctx.tenant_id, result["cost_inr"]) latency = round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1) trace.update(output={"answer": result["answer"][:500], "n_citations": len(result["citations"]), "latency_ms": latency}) return QueryResult( answer=result["answer"], citations=result["citations"], trace_id=trace.id, request_id=request_id, route=route, cache_status="miss", cost_inr=result["cost_inr"], latency_ms=latency, system_fingerprint=self.version.fingerprint) ``` **Returning `trace_id` to the caller** is what makes "this answer was wrong" actionable — Day 35's point, and the thing the Pune team lacked. **The order — budget, input guard, cache, route, retrieve, generate, output guard — is deliberate.** Cheap checks first, cache before any expensive work, guards on both ends. ##### Build order ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1. Design doc
+ capacity model"] --> B["2. Repo scaffold
+ config + CI"] B --> C["3. Ingestion
+ inspect chunks"] C --> D["4. Golden eval set
120 cases"] D --> E["5. Naive retrieval
MEASURE baseline"] E --> F["6. Security context
+ access tests"] F --> G["7. Generation
+ citations"] G --> H["8. Improve retrieval
measure each change"] H --> I["9. Tracing + metrics"] I --> J["10. Guards + budget"] J --> K["Part 2: optimise,
deploy, harden"] ``` **Step 4 before step 5.** Building the evaluation set before optimising is what turns every subsequent change into a measured number rather than a guess — the Day 43 beginner-track point, and it matters more at this scale. **Step 6 early, not late.** Access control retrofitted into a working system is how the Pune leak happened. Build the `SecurityContext` before the retriever, so there is never a code path without it. ##### The evaluation set ```python # eval/build_golden_set.py from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict import json GOLDEN_SET_COMPOSITION = { "extraction": 30, # direct lookup "reasoning": 24, # inference from one document "multi_hop": 18, # requires 2+ documents "unanswerable": 24, # MUST refuse — highest value "access_control": 12, # must not retrieve across tenants "adversarial": 12, # injection attempts } @dataclass class GoldenCase: id: str category: str question: str tenant_id: str expected_chunk_ids: list[str] reference_answer: str | None must_contain: list[str] | None must_not_contain: list[str] | None should_refuse: bool difficulty: str def validate_golden_set(cases: list[GoldenCase]) -> dict: from collections import Counter counts = Counter(c.category for c in cases) issues = [] for cat, target in GOLDEN_SET_COMPOSITION.items(): if counts[cat] < target * 0.8: issues.append(f"{cat}: {counts[cat]} cases, target {target}") refusal_cases = [c for c in cases if c.should_refuse] if len(refusal_cases) / len(cases) < 0.15: issues.append("fewer than 15% refusal cases — hallucination " "regressions will go undetected") return {"total": len(cases), "by_category": dict(counts), "issues": issues} ``` **24 unanswerable cases out of 120.** That is 20%, and it is the category that catches the failure mode users complain about most — Day 36's Pune prompt regression would have been blocked by these. **12 access-control cases** verify the tenant filter with real queries, not just unit tests. ##### The Part 1 checklist - [ ] Design document with quantified non-functional requirements - [ ] Architecture diagram with a one-line justification per component - [ ] Capacity and cost model, validated against the budget - [ ] Sensitivity analysis identifying the dominant cost driver - [ ] Repository scaffolded with `docs/`, `eval/`, `tests/` - [ ] Configuration centralised, secrets failing fast - [ ] Model snapshots pinned, `SystemVersion` fingerprint implemented - [ ] Ingestion pipeline with chunks inspected by hand - [ ] Golden set of 100+ cases, 15%+ unanswerable, built before optimising - [ ] Baseline measured and recorded - [ ] `SecurityContext` with pre-filter and post-verify - [ ] Access control tests including the deliberately-broken-filter case - [ ] Generation with citations and a working refusal path - [ ] Tracing wired with `trace_id` returned to callers - [ ] `make setup && make ingest && make serve` works from a clean clone ##### Common mistakes - **Designing the happy path only** — the 31-second Wednesday. - **No capacity model**, discovering the cost problem in week seven. - **Access control added after the retriever works.** - **No evaluation set before optimising**, so improvements are guesses. - **Architecture decisions with no `revisit_if` trigger.** - **A dedicated vector database for 180,000 chunks** when pgvector suffices. - **Model aliases instead of pinned snapshots.** - **No `trace_id` returned**, making complaints unactionable. - **Fewer than 15% unanswerable cases** in the golden set. - **Configuration scattered across modules** rather than one settings object. - **Runbooks left for later** — they are part of the design, not documentation debt. ##### Hands-on: write the numbers down Your practical task is the system design document plus repository scaffold. **Fill in the non-functional table with real numbers derived from your user count and usage assumptions**, then run the capacity model. If the projected cost exceeds your budget, resolve it in the design — smaller model, higher cache hit rate, fewer chunks — rather than discovering it later. The mini project builds the core: ingestion through generation with access control and tracing. Follow the build order, and resist skipping step 4. The moment you have a baseline number, every subsequent change becomes an experiment with a result rather than a hopeful improvement. The assignment implements the core pipeline with evaluation and tracing under version control. "Under version control" means specifics: pinned dependencies, a `SystemVersion` fingerprint on every trace, a golden set committed to the repo, and a baseline JSON that the regression gate compares against. A reviewer should be able to clone, run `make eval`, and reproduce your numbers. ##### Key takeaways - **Quantified non-functional requirements are what make it a design** — peak QPS, TTFT p95, cost budget, and accuracy floor each constrain a specific architectural choice. - **Run the capacity and cost model before writing code.** Discovering a 4× budget overrun on day one is a design decision; discovering it in week seven is a crisis. - **Justify every component in one sentence and attach a `revisit_if` trigger**, or the architecture accumulates rather than being designed. - **Build access control before the retriever**, with pre-filter, post-verify, and a test that deliberately breaks the primary control. - **Build the golden evaluation set before optimising anything**, with at least 15% unanswerable cases — it is what turns every later change into a measured result.
practical_task_reference: Write a system design doc (requirements, architecture, data flow, SLAs, cost model) and scaffold the repository.
mini_project_reference: Build the core of a production GenAI application, for example an enterprise knowledge platform with agentic RAG.
assignment_reference: Implement the core pipeline with an evaluation harness and tracing wired in, under version control.
